microtopics.title: Polynomial Interpolation, Degree Bounds, and Vanishing Cosets
microtopics.badge_reason: Establishing when finite point agreement guarantees polynomial identity requires coordinating degree bounds with algebraic cosets.
entry_assumptions: Factor Theorem for finding linear factors (x - r).
microtopics.inferential_jump: Agreement of polynomials at k inputs proves identity if and only if their degrees are strictly less than k; otherwise, solutions form an infinite coset parameterized by the product of linear factors.

teaching_path.action: Inspect finite data sample points and formulate a candidate interpolating polynomial.
teaching_path.why_valid: Evaluation identifies a low-degree polynomial that matches the given sample points.

teaching_path.action: Form the difference polynomial d(x) = p(x) - q(x) and count its distinct zeros.
teaching_path.why_valid: Each agreement point x_i is a root of the difference polynomial d(x_i) = 0.
teaching_path.output: factored difference polynomial with known roots

teaching_path.action: Apply the degree bound: if deg(d) < number of distinct roots, d(x) is identically zero.
teaching_path.why_valid: A non-zero polynomial of degree n can have at most n roots by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.

teaching_path.action: Remove the degree bound and express the general solution as an affine coset modulo the vanishing product.
teaching_path.why_valid: Any polynomial vanishing on the sample set is an arbitrary polynomial multiple of the vanishing product.

construction_units.decision: Determine when finite data uniquely determine a polynomial and characterize all solutions when the degree bound is removed

independent_checks.statement: CHECK: Prove why 4 points uniquely fix a cubic polynomial but leave a quartic polynomial underdetermined.
APPLY: If p and q have degree <= 3 and agree at -1, 0, 1 with p(2)-q(2)=12, find p(3)-q(3).
CONNECT: Refute the heuristic that agreement at 3 inputs always proves an identity.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A polynomial matching n data points is always unique without requiring a degree bound.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If p(x) fits 4 data points, does that automatically mean p(x) must be a quadratic or cubic?
misconceptions.repair: Uniqueness requires deg(p) <= n - 1; without a degree bound, infinitely many higher-degree polynomials match the same points.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Agreement at three points proves that two functions are identical.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can two different degree-3 polynomials agree at three distinct values?
misconceptions.repair: Agreement at 3 points proves identity only for polynomials of degree at most 2. For degree 3, they differ by c*(x-x1)(x-x2)(x-3).

exit_task.prompt: Polynomials f and g have degree at most 3. They agree at x = 1, 2, 3, and f(4) - g(4) = 18. Find f(0) - g(0).

reasoning: Difference polynomial has degree <= 3 and roots 1, 2, 3.
Evaluating at x = 4 fixes leading coefficient c = 3.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The task verifies degree-bounded difference interpolation.

microtopics.research_contribution: Addresses Q1, Q8, and Q10 on polynomial interpolation uniqueness, difference polynomials, and qualified decision procedures.

predict.prompt: If a polynomial matches four data points, is it unique without a degree bound?
predict.defensible_answer: No, without a degree bound there is an infinite family of solutions.

rubric.criterion: Identifies that uniqueness requires degree <= 3 for 4 points.

accepted: Difference d(x) = x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)q(x) satisfies all four data points for any polynomial q(x).
rejected: p(x) = x^2 + 1 is the only polynomial that can ever fit these points.

route.ask: What polynomial of degree 4 vanishes at all four data x-coordinates 0, 1, 2, 3?
route.why_this_ask: Isolates the degree-4 vanishing product that generates the null space of evaluations.

route.ask: If a quartic polynomial p(x) matches the four points, how does p(x) relate to the quadratic interpolant x^2 + 1?
route.why_this_ask: Forces realization that p(x) - (x^2 + 1) must be a multiple of the vanishing product.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: Learners explore the non-uniqueness of unconstrained interpolants constructively via the null space rather than beginning with the degree-bounded uniqueness theorem.

boundary_test.prompt: Suppose five data points are given. What is the maximum degree a polynomial can have while still being guaranteed unique by the data?
boundary_test.confirms: Confirms mastery of the degree bound n - 1 versus the number of points n.
boundary_test.answer: Degree at most 4. By the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, two distinct polynomials of degree <= 4 can agree at at most 4 points unless they are identical.

microtopics.title: Root Multiplicity Parity, Sign Trapping, and Minimal Degree
microtopics.badge_reason: Hardest target in the cohort: proving minimal degree requires coordinating IVT sign trapping, root multiplicity parity, and irreducible quadratic discriminant constraints.
entry_assumptions: Factor Theorem and definition of root multiplicity.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A real polynomial changes sign across a real root if and only if its multiplicity is odd; if a polynomial is positive on both sides of an isolated zero, the root must have even multiplicity (at least 2), and any quadratic factor with no real roots maintains a strictly constant sign.

teaching_path.action: Connect sign variation across zeros to multiplicity parity: odd multiplicity crosses the axis; even multiplicity is tangent without sign change.
teaching_path.why_valid: Near root r of multiplicity m, p(x) ~ k(x-r)^m, whose sign flips iff m is odd.

teaching_path.action: Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem to trap root signs: positive values on both sides of a zero force even multiplicity to prevent intermediate zeros.
teaching_path.why_valid: If a simple zero changed sign between two positive evaluations, IVT would force another zero, violating given root count.

teaching_path.action: Evaluate quadratic factor irreducibility: an irreducible quadratic has negative discriminant and constant sign on R.
teaching_path.why_valid: If Delta = b^2 - 4ac < 0, ax^2 + bx + c never vanishes and has the constant sign of a.

teaching_path.action: Construct explicit minimal-degree polynomial satisfying all constraints and prove all smaller degrees impossible.
teaching_path.why_valid: Systematic elimination of degrees 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 establishes degree 5 as the exact minimal degree.
teaching_path.output: minimal degree proof and verified specimen

construction_units.decision: Deduce root multiplicities from sign behavior across zeros, prove degrees 1-4 impossible via IVT and quadratic sign constraints, and construct a verified degree-5 polynomial

independent_checks.statement: CHECK: Prove why p(0)=1>0, p(2)=1>0, and p(1)=0 prevents 1 from being a root of multiplicity 1.
APPLY: If p is monic with distinct real zeros strictly +/-1 and p(0)=1, prove no irreducible quadratic factor can be present.
CONNECT: Verify that 3x^2 - 10x + 12 has discriminant -44 < 0 and is strictly positive on all of R.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every zero of a polynomial must be a simple zero (multiplicity 1).
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can a polynomial touch the x-axis and turn around without crossing it?
misconceptions.repair: A root has even multiplicity (2, 4, ...) when the curve is tangent to the axis without crossing; crossing with sign change occurs only for odd multiplicities.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any four given values can always be fitted by a degree 3 or degree 4 polynomial with prescribed real zeros.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If a quadratic factor has no real roots, can it change sign between x = 0 and x = 2?
misconceptions.repair: An irreducible quadratic has constant sign across all real numbers. When multiplied by (x^2 - 1), it forces p(0) and p(2) to have opposite signs, making degree 4 impossible.

exit_task.prompt: Find the least possible degree of a real polynomial with zeros strictly at x = 2, which satisfies p(1) = 3 and p(3) = 3. Exhibit one such polynomial.

answer.summary: Least possible degree is 2. Since p(1) = 3 > 0 and p(3) = 3 > 0 with zero at 2, mult(2) must be even (mult >= 2) to avoid crossing 0 and creating intermediate roots. At degree 2, p(x) = c(x - 2)^2. Setting p(1) = c(1-2)^2 = c = 3 gives p(x) = 3(x - 2)^2. Check p(3) = 3(3-2)^2 = 3. Only zero is x = 2.
reasoning: Sign preservation at 1 and 3 requires even multiplicity at 2.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The task verifies minimal degree under sign preservation.

microtopics.research_contribution: Addresses Q2, Q3, and Q9 on root multiplicity parity, IVT sign trapping, and complete monic polynomial characterization.

predict.prompt: Can a polynomial of degree 4 have real roots only at -1 and 1 and satisfy p(0)=1, p(2)=1?
predict.defensible_answer: No, because any irreducible quadratic maintains constant sign, forcing p(0) and p(2) to have opposite signs.

rubric.criterion: Eliminates degree 3 via IVT sign trapping at 1.
Eliminates degree 4 by showing quadratic factor has constant sign.
rubric.evidence_of: Coordinates factor sign with evaluation values.

accepted: Degree 5 is the least degree; explicit polynomial (1/12)(x-1)^2(x+1)(3x^2-10x+12) satisfies all conditions.
rejected: Degree 3 or 4 is sufficient by Lagrange interpolation.

task.prompt: Prove that degree 4 is impossible for Q3.

route.ask: What is the sign of the product (x+1)(x-1) on the interval between 0 and 2?
route.why_this_ask: Exposes that (0+1)(0-1) = -1 < 0 while (2+1)(2-1) = 3 > 0, flipping sign across x = 1.

route.ask: Can an irreducible quadratic factor Q(x) with Delta < 0 change sign between x = 0 and x = 2 to compensate?
route.why_this_ask: Demonstrates that Q(x) has strictly constant sign on all real numbers, making degree 4 impossible.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: Learners discover the obstruction to degree 4 by testing factor sign behavior directly at the evaluation points rather than through general discriminant theorems.

boundary_test.prompt: Can a polynomial with real roots only at -1 and 1 satisfy p(0) = -1 and p(2) = 3 with degree 2?
boundary_test.confirms: Confirms understanding of how signs at test points constrain the leading coefficient and root parity.
boundary_test.answer: Yes; p(x) = x^2 - 1 has degree 2, zeros at +/-1, p(0) = -1, and p(2) = 3.

microtopics.title: Parameter Bifurcations, Geometric Modeling, and Domain Preservation
microtopics.badge_reason: Requires coordinating algebraic parameter case splits with physical geometric modeling and rigorous function domain constraints.
entry_assumptions: Algebraic grouping and factoring of polynomial expressions.
Geometric formulas for rectangular box volume.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A parameter variation can cause leading terms to vanish (dropping the degree) or roots to collide (changing multiplicities); an empirical fit matching sample points may violate geometric domain constraints.

teaching_path.action: Group and factor polynomial expressions with parameters to isolate fixed zeros and variable factors.
teaching_path.why_valid: Factoring F_a(x) into x(x+2)[(a-1)x^2 + (a+2)] isolates fixed roots 0, -2 and parameter-dependent quadratic.

teaching_path.action: Identify critical parameter values where the leading coefficient vanishes (degree drop) or roots coincide (multiplicity increase).
teaching_path.why_valid: Leading coefficient a-1=0 drops degree from 4 to 2 at a=1; roots merge at a=-2 (triple zero) and a=2/5 (double zero at -2).

teaching_path.action: Derive geometric polynomial models from physical constraints and evaluate non-degenerate domains.
teaching_path.why_valid: Folded box has V(x) = x(10-2x)^2 on (0, 5); fitted quadratic Q(x) produces unphysical negative volumes.
teaching_path.output: geometric model vs empirical fit critique

teaching_path.action: Enforce domain preservation for rational expressions under algebraic cancellation.
teaching_path.why_valid: Cancelling (x-a)/(x-a) preserves domain restriction x != a; extending to R is a separate mathematical operation.

construction_units.decision: Classify degree drops and root coincidences under parameter variation, critique empirical polynomial fits against geometric physics, and enforce domain preservation

independent_checks.statement: CHECK: Show why F_a(x) drops from degree 4 to degree 2 at a = 1.
APPLY: At x = 3 cm, calculate physical box volume V(3) versus analyst quadratic Q(3).
CONNECT: Explain why R_1(x) = (x-1)^2/(x-1) has no real zeros on its original domain.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The largest printed exponent is always the degree of a polynomial.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What is the degree of (a - 1)x^4 + 3x^2 when a = 1?
misconceptions.repair: The degree is the highest exponent with a non-zero coefficient. If a parameter causes the leading coefficient to vanish, the degree drops.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Cancelling common factors in a rational expression makes it a polynomial function on all real numbers.
misconceptions.repair: Algebraic cancellation is valid only on the original domain where the denominator is non-zero. A removable singularity requires a continuous extension.

exit_task.prompt: For what real value of k does G_k(x) = (k^2 - 4)x^3 + (k - 2)x^2 + 5x - 1 have degree 1? Explain.

answer.summary: Degree 1 requires the coefficients of x^3 and x^2 to vanish simultaneously, while the coefficient of x is non-zero (5 != 0). k^2 - 4 = 0 => k = 2 or -2. k - 2 = 0 => k = 2. Both vanish simultaneously if and only if k = 2. At k = 2, G_2(x) = 5x - 1, which has degree 1.
reasoning: Coefficient of x^3 must be zero: k in {2, -2}.
Coefficient of x^2 must be zero: k = 2.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The task assesses parameter degree drop.

microtopics.research_contribution: Addresses Q4, Q5, Q6, and Q7 on parameter bifurcations, cubic geometric box modeling, rational domain preservation, and even symmetry.

predict.prompt: What is the degree of F_a(x) when a = 1?
predict.defensible_answer: Degree 2, because both x^4 and x^3 coefficients vanish.

rubric.criterion: Identifies root coincidences at a = -2 and a = 2/5.

accepted: F_a factors as x(x+2)[(a-1)x^2 + (a+2)]; degree drops to 2 at a=1; roots coincide at a=-2 (triple root at 0) and a=2/5 (double root at -2).
rejected: F_a always has degree 4 and 4 distinct zeros.

task.prompt: Classify all exceptional values of a for F_a(x).

route.ask: What happens to the degree of F_a(x) = (a-1)x^4 + 2(a-1)x^3 + (a+2)x^2 + 2(a+2)x when a = 1?
route.why_this_ask: Exposes the coefficient of x^4 and x^3 becoming 0 simultaneously, dropping the degree to 2.

route.ask: Under what condition does the quadratic factor (a-1)x^2 + (a+2) share a root with x(x+2)?
route.why_this_ask: Leads the learner to substitute x = 0 and x = -2 into the quadratic factor to discover parameter bifurcations.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: Learners isolate root collisions and degree drops by direct substitution into factored sub-expressions rather than abstract discriminant formulas.

boundary_test.prompt: For what value of a does the quadratic factor (a-1)x^2 + (a+2) have no real roots?
boundary_test.confirms: Confirms ability to solve parameter inequalities for root existence.
boundary_test.answer: When -(a+2)/(a-1) < 0, which occurs for a > 1 or a < -2.

relations.meaning: If polynomials p and q agree at k distinct inputs, their difference is divisible by the degree-k vanishing product; if deg(p-q) < k, then p = q identically.
conditions: p, q are polynomials with real coefficients.
Points x_1, ..., x_k are pairwise distinct.

derivation.why_valid: Difference of polynomials is a polynomial.

derivation.action: Apply Factor Theorem at each agreement point x_i.
derivation.output: product of linear factors divides d(x)

derivation.action: Compare degree of d with k: if deg(d) < k, d(x) = 0 identically.
derivation.why_valid: A nonzero polynomial of degree < k cannot have k roots.

limits: Does not hold for general transcendental functions.
Requires exact agreement without rounding error.
checks: Verify that with 4 points, a cubic is unique while a quartic has a free parameter.

relations.meaning: A polynomial changes sign across an isolated real root r if and only if its multiplicity m is odd; if m is even, the sign is preserved.

derivation.action: Write p(x) = (x - r)^m g(x) with g(r) != 0.
Evaluate sign of (x - r)^m as x passes through r.
derivation.why_valid: (x - r)^m changes sign iff m is odd.

derivation.action: Since g(r) != 0, g(x) maintains constant sign in a neighborhood of r.

checks: Verify x^2 does not change sign across 0; x^3 changes sign across 0.

relations.expression: \Delta = b^2 - 4ac < 0 \implies ax^2 + bx + c \text{ has constant sign on } \mathbb{R}
relations.meaning: A real quadratic with negative discriminant has no real roots and maintains a constant non-zero sign across all real numbers.
conditions: a != 0, a, b, c in R.

derivation.action: Complete the square: ax^2 + bx + c = a(x + b/(2a))^2 - Delta/(4a).
If Delta < 0, -Delta/(4a) has the same sign as a.
Conclude expression has the same sign as a for all real x.
derivation.why_valid: Square is non-negative, offset is strictly positive in sign of a.

checks: Verify x^2 + bx - 1 has Delta = b^2 + 4 > 0, always possessing real roots.

relations.meaning: Volume of an open box formed by cutting corner squares of side x from an L x L square sheet, valid on physical domain 0 < x < L/2.

derivation.action: Identify height of folded box as x.
derivation.why_valid: Folding flaps creates height equal to corner cutout.

derivation.action: Compute base dimensions: length = width = L - 2x.
derivation.why_valid: Cutting two corners of size x reduces length by 2x.

derivation.action: Multiply base area by height to obtain cubic volume formula.
derivation.why_valid: Volume of rectangular cuboid is base area times height.

question_families.title: Polynomials in One Variable with Real Coefficients — Competition Stress Family
solution_structure: State exact givens and identify degree bounds and domain restrictions.
Factor expressions or form differences to expose root structures.
Apply multiplicity parity, IVT, and discriminant constraints to bound degrees.
Synthesize unique solutions or characterize infinite cosets with model boundaries.

demand_dimensions.model_choice: Choose between degree-bounded uniqueness, affine cosets, multiplicity parity, and physical cubic modeling.
demand_dimensions.representation_translation: Translate sign behaviors and geometric box cuts into algebraic polynomial constraints.
demand_dimensions.reasoning_steps: Givens, root factoring, degree bounding, IVT/discriminant test, unique/coset synthesis.
demand_dimensions.novelty: Minimal degree 5 proof, parameter bifurcation at a=2/5, rational cancellation domain fallacy.

safe_variations: Vary numerical values while preserving topological sign trapping and degree bounds.
transfer_boundaries: Do not apply finite interpolation uniqueness without degree bounds.
Do not cancel rational factors without preserving domain restrictions.
common_wrong_routes: Claiming interpolation uniqueness without degree bounds.
Assuming all roots are simple roots (multiplicity 1).
Equating rational expressions to polynomials across all real numbers.
